title: Owen Ndlovu: Abducted South African journalist found dead with gunshot wounds
description: Provincial police spokesperson Col Dimakatso Nevhuhulwi said Ndlovu had gone to pick up his wife from a religious service when the attackers struck."A
body: Provincial police spokesperson Col Dimakatso Nevhuhulwi said Ndlovu had gone to pick up his wife from a religious service when the attackers struck."As she approached their vehicle, three unknown men, one reportedly armed with a firearm, suddenly approached them, pushed her aside and forced her husband into the back seat," she said."The suspects then drove off with the victim."The vehicle, a Ford Raptor pick-up truck - commonly known as a bakkie in South Africa - was later recovered abandoned in Walkerville, an area south of Johannesburg, police said.Ndlovu's body was found by local residents beside a road in Thokoza, which neighbours Katlehong. They said he appeared to have suffered gunshot wounds. A bag of his was found a few metres away.Police said they were investigating a case of murder but a post-mortem examination would establish the cause of death."At this stage, the family is awaiting further information from the relevant authorities regarding the circumstances surrounding Owen's death," said family spokesperson Eugene Mthethwa.The family described the loss as "devastating" and thanked residents, police and members of the public who had helped search for him after news of his abduction emerged.Ndlovu was a familiar figure to South African sports fans after years working as a presenter and producer at the SABC.He was also involved in radio coverage of the country's Premier Soccer League and later became an advocate for musicians' rights and royalty payments. The 54-year-old was also associated with Artists United and the SABC Summer Song of the Year initiative.Lelo Mzaca, a fellow journalist, remembered him as a man who lived a "colourful, energetic life" and brought enthusiasm and flair to sports broadcasting."South Africa has lost a unique and spirited individual whose light shone brightly while it lasted," Mzaca added in a tribute on the Mail & Guardian news site.The provincial government urged communities to help police with the investigation, saying tackling crime remained a priority. The killing has again drawn attention to violent crime in South Africa, where armed robberies and vehicle hijackings remain a major concern. The latest national police figures, covering April to June 2026, recorded more than 5,000 murders and close to 4,000 carjackings. When releasing the figures last month, acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia said serious crimes continued to create fear in communities and that some were carried out by "organised, heavily armed criminal groups that operate with planning and sophistication".

schema.headline: Owen Ndlovu: Abducted South African journalist found dead with gunshot wounds

title: Australia immigration crackdown: visas for international students and backpackers targeted
description: International students, so-called "visa hoppers" and backpackers will be targeted under stricter rules announced by Australia on Thursday in a bid to
body: International students, so-called "visa hoppers" and backpackers will be targeted under stricter rules announced by Australia on Thursday in a bid to curb immigration.Foreign students will no longer be able to bring their families with them and those who want to extend their stay must choose a higher qualification.Rules will also be stricter for working holiday visas - commonly used by backpackers and a crucial labour source for the agricultural sector - with a ballot system although these changes will not affect the UK.The new rules were revealed by Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke who said that while immigration was a "strength" of Australia, there needed to be a "high level of control".For international student and graduate visas, Burke said: "We will no longer be adding to the stock of students automatically being able to bring family members over."There would be exemptions for foreign students already in Australia as well as applicants from the Pacific and South East Asian countries, he said.PhD students would also be able to bring their families as they were in different life circumstances to undergraduates, Burke said. In a speech titled "The work of managing the migration program: who arrives, who stays, who leaves", Burke revealed a raft of changes as the government aims to bring net overseas migration to 225,000 people by 2028.On student visas, he said the government would clamp down on "visa hopping" - where a student finishes a course, then applies to do another course which is often a lower qualification and sometimes with a "not so legitimate provider".Students who want to go "up the scale" will be allowed, Burke said, for example, if a student finishes a bachelor's degree and then wants to complete a masters.He also announced major changes to working holiday visas for those aged 18 to 30 years old who can work in Australia for 12 months, but can extend for a second and third year. Currently, these visa holders must work for three months in regional Australia during their first year to qualify for a second year, and then six months to qualify for a third year.Under the new changes, those who qualify for a second year will have to go into a ballot with a cap of 45,000, down from the 57,000 who qualified last year.For the third year, the ballot will be limited to 5,000, down from 31,000 who qualified last year. British working holidaymakers will not be affected by these changes due to the UK's free trade agreement with Australia.New figures released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics on Thursday showed Australia's population grew 1.4% in the 12 months to March 2026 to 27.9m.That total figure included births and deaths as well as a net overseas migration of 292,100. Migration remains a major political issue as debate around Australia's population grows amid rising living costs, housing affordability and increased strain on public services.One Nation, a populist right-wing party known for its anti-immigration stance and which has seen a surge in support in recent months, detailed its migration policy earlier this week, proposing to cut temporary migrant visas by 750,000 over three years.The party, which won its first lower house seat in May, also wants to cap net overseas immigration to 130,000, drawing a rebuke from Burke who said such a proposal would risk "smashing parts of the Australian economy".In July, the government introduced a policy to prioritise applications for family visas  lodged onshore - where the applicant is in the country already - over those submitted overseas. Skilled migrants already in Australia who applied for permanent visas were also prioritised over those applying from overseas.It also paused applications for working holiday visas from 24 countries, not including the UK.Violet Roumeliotis, from Settlement Services International which helps new arrivals to Australia, says the migration debate was increasingly driven by "short-term politics rather than what is best for the country". "The proposed changes to family visas for international students is a good example of this," she said, adding that it would make it harder for Australia to compete for "future talent".

schema.headline: Australia immigration crackdown: visas for international students and backpackers targeted

title: Charlie Kirk's family alleges 'stunning failures' by Utah officials led to his shooting
description: Charlie Kirk's family has accused the Utah Valley University and state officials of "stunning failures and reckless decisions" that they say led to th
body: Charlie Kirk's family has accused the Utah Valley University and state officials of "stunning failures and reckless decisions" that they say led to the conservative activist's 2025 assassination during a campus event.In a legal notice, lawyers for the family say Kirk's Turning Point USA event at the university campus was not properly secured or monitored, making him an easy target.Kirk, 31, was speaking to a crowd of thousands on the university campus, when he was shot and killed by a gunman positioned on a roof.The university said it was aware of the claim but did not comment further on the allegations, according to a statement shared with the BBC's US partner CBS News. "We are aware of the notice of claim. UVU addresses legal matters consistent with our established processes, " the university said in its statement. "Our focus remains on supporting our campus community."The legal notice was filed on 9 September, a day ahead of the one-year anniversary of Kirk's death, and is typically a precursor to a lawsuit. It names Utah Valley University, local police, the state of Utah, and other university officials as parties who were allegedly aware of the threats against Kirk and did not take steps to protect him."Through a series of stunning failures and reckless decisions, the UVU Parties created a foreseeable danger to Charlie," the notice alleges."Placing a politically controversial figure like Charlie Kirk in an outdoor event in the quad surrounded by tall buildings and other elevated observation platforms is accurately described as walking him into a fishbowl," it says.Kirk's family alleges the university failed to conduct a meaningful security assessment ahead of the event, failed to assign enough police officers, and did not have an ambulance available on site. The family also alleges the  university ignored warnings about securing the rooftops surrounding the courtyard where Kirk was speaking. "The risk of a rooftop shooter should have been especially top-of-mind given the attempted assassination of President Trump, Charlie Kirk's close friend and political ally, by a rooftop shooter the previous year," the family's attorney D Loren Washburn wrote in the court filing.Tyler Robinson, a 23-year-old man from Utah, who has been accused of shooting Kirk from a roof, is due to appear in court next month to hear the date of his trial. Robinson denies aggravated murder, a capital offence in the state, as well as six other charges.Prosecutors have called for the death penalty.

schema.headline: Charlie Kirk's family alleges 'stunning failures' by Utah officials led to his shooting

title: Trump chief of staff Susie Wiles announces she's cancer-free
description: White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles has announced she is free of cancer, exactly six months after she announced her diagnosis. In a post on X, Wile
body: White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles has announced she is free of cancer, exactly six months after she announced her diagnosis. In a post on X, Wiles said her pathology tests "came back clear" after a visit to the Mayo Clinic earlier this week. Wiles, 69, is considered among the most powerful figures in the Trump administration and someone particularly close to the US president. In her post, Wiles thanked Trump for his "unwavering support" and vowed to continue working to "advance his America First Agenda". Wiles continued working virtually at the White House during the six months of treatment following her diagnosis.In a March statement, Wiles said that one in eight women are diagnosed with breast cancer."Every day, these women continue to raise their families, go to work and serve their communities with strength and determination," she said. "I now join their ranks."Her post on Wednesday did not reveal any more details about her treatment.Wiles is the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff - widely considered to be the most important role in the White House.In her position, Wiles works to keep the president's agenda on track and serves as a gatekeeper to President Trump, as well as a policy coordinator and political advisor.Before taking the job, Wiles played a significant role in President Trump's 2024 presidential campaign.Her tenure, however, has not been without controversy.In December, Vanity Fair published interviews with Wiles in which she gave a blunt - and occasionally unflattering - assessment of her time working in the Trump White House.For example, she described the famously teetotaling president as having an "alcoholic's personality" but added that there's "nothing he can't do. Nothing, zero, nothing."She also provided candid thoughts about other figures close to the US president, describing Vice-President JD Vance as a "conspiracy theorist" and Elon Musk as an "odd, odd duck."The US president, however, swiftly came to her defence and Wiles described Vanity Fair's reporting as having omitted "significant context" to create a "chaotic and negative narrative" about the administration.President Trump and the White House have yet to comment on Wiles' announcement.

schema.headline: Trump chief of staff Susie Wiles announces she's cancer-free

title: Colombia and Brazil deadliest countries for environmental defenders, report says
description: Colombia has again topped the list of countries with the highest number of killings of land and environmental activists, according to an annual report
body: Colombia has again topped the list of countries with the highest number of killings of land and environmental activists, according to an annual report by campaign group Global Witness, external. Out of at least 124 activists killed globally in 2025, 39 were murdered in Colombia, followed by Brazil with 26.Global Witness says that 85% of the documented killings took place in Latin America, making it the deadliest region for every year since the group started publishing its reports in 2012. Most of the killings were part of land disputes and in many cases they were carried out by hitmen or members of organised crime gangs, the report states.Colombia has accounted for the highest number of murders of environmental activists for the past four years. Almost half of those killed in the country were members of indigenous groups, while many of the remaining ones were small-scale farmers, Global Witness's report says.Many indigenous groups in Colombia have created their own protection networks in the form of indigenous guards, which patrol their territory but are unarmed. Members of indigenous guards are often targeted by illegal armed groups looking to expand their territory to plant coca - the raw material used to make cocaine - or to engage in illegal mining. Last week, Jacob Guachetá Zambrano, who was part of the indigenous guard in Colombia's Cauca region, was found tortured and killed.While the possible motive behind his murder is still under investigation and the search for the perpetrator is ongoing, indigenous leaders said that murders, threats and forced disappearances in the area were common as illegal armed groups battled for territory. Global Witness warned that Brazil had seen a doubling of killings of environmental defenders in 2025 compared to 2024. As in Colombia, in Brazil most of the cases the group documented were primarily driven by conflict over land, Global Witness's researchers found. Outside of Latin America, 12% of the murders occurred in Asia, with Philippines top of the list with 12 documented murders. The group warned that while globally the number of documented killings had gone down from 146 in 2024 to 128 in 2025, its numbers were probably an underestimate as many cases went unreported.

schema.headline: Colombia and Brazil deadliest countries for environmental defenders, report says

title: DoJ accuses Russia of trying to kill Ukraine allies in US and Europe
description: The US Department of Justice (DoJ) has accused Russia of plotting to murder Ukrainian allies in the US and Europe. In a statement on Tuesday, the DoJ
body: The US Department of Justice (DoJ) has accused Russia of plotting to murder Ukrainian allies in the US and Europe. In a statement on Tuesday, the DoJ charged five men allegedly connected to the Russian Intelligence Services (RIS). The men are accused of paying, or trying to pay, people in the US and overseas to target those "aligned, or perceived to be aligned, with Ukraine"."It is our job to stop America's adversaries from unleashing violence and terror on American soil," Attorney General Todd Blanche. All those accused remain at large. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Wednesday Moscow will not comment until it hears or sees "any credible evidence" or "tangible facts".It is not clear if the five accused are in the United States, or in a different location. Washington has charged all five men with participating in a conspiracy to finance terrorism, which carries a maximum 20-year prison sentence.Three of the defendants are "high-ranking members of the RIS network", the DoJ said.Among them are Russian father and son Yuri Khrameev, 63, and Kirill Khrameev, 27. Khrameev senior was a colonel in the Russian intelligence services and his son is an officer in the Federal Security Service of Russia (FSB).The third high-ranking suspect is Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, a 35-year-old Cuban national who the US describe as "an influential member of the Cuban diaspora living in Russia who has coordinated attacks for the RIS network". Yaidel Delgado Suarez, 35, and Angel Eduardo Castro, 22, are the other two defendants. The pair are accused of recruiting or attempting to recruit US-based individuals to "surveil and attempt to murder a prominent US-based Russian dissident".The FBI's James Barnacle said the group "conspired to intimidate, threaten, or murder people on US soil and around the world".One of the incidents is as recent as this summer. The DoJ described how the RIS network was able to recruit someone in the US to surveil and eventually murder a Russian dissident in the US.Suarez allegedly sent the recruit to two locations linked to the victim with "explicit instructions on how to conduct surveillance". In exchange, the recruit was offered between $1,000 (£743) and $1,500.Suarez and Castro are said to have offered an additional $40,000 if the US resident could "eliminate" the dissident.The DoJ said the RIS recruit did not go through with it, which led Suarez to try and recruit "multiple other individuals within the United States". He allegedly offered "substantial sums of money to carry out the targeting of US based victims".The release by the DoJ goes on to list other instances in which the accused allegedly tried to recruit others to kill those who were a perceived threat to Russia. It said that in 2025, Khrameev junior allegedly recruited a US citizen to surveil and murder someone in Lithuania who was "telling lies about Russia". The release quotes Khrameev as saying the purpose was to target "all the countries that are helping Ukraine". His father, Khrameev senior, is said to have offered the recruit $25,000 to kill the individual in Lithuania for "spreading dirt about my country" and "distorting history". Khrameev senior, Suarez and Castro are the only ones also charged with "participating in a conspiracy to commit murder for hire". If found guilty, this charge carries a maximum 10-year prison sentence.It is not the first time authorities thwart threats of this kind.Last month, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said authorities had detained an individual allegedly working for the Kremlin and who was plotting to murder an American-Ukrainian citizen in Warsaw.Tusk told reporters the American-Ukrainian citizen "was uncomfortable for the Putin regime", adding: "We have to accept the assumption that the Putin regime will try to eliminate people who are inconvenient for various reasons."In 2024, German authorities were reportedly warned by US intelligence of a Russian plot to kill Armin Papperger, the head of Germany's biggest arms company Rheinmetall.Moscow dismissed the accusation at the time, with Kremlin spokesman Peskov saying: "It's all presented in the style of another fake story, so such reports cannot be taken seriously."The fresh accusations from the DoJ come at a time of closer relations between Moscow and Washington following US President Donald Trump's return to the White House in 2025.A few weeks ago, the head of the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) visited Moscow for talks with figures from Russia's intelligence services - an unconventional move that led to speculation.The Kremlin confirmed that talks between John Ratcliffe and the intelligence services had taken place. President Trump did not say what was discussed but described the meeting as "semi-routine".

schema.headline: DoJ accuses Russia of trying to kill Ukraine allies in US and Europe

title: Saudi Arabia says it shot down Houthi drone south of Mecca
description: Saudi Arabia intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone south of the Islamic holy city of Mecca on Tuesday evening, according to the spokesman of the Sa
body: Saudi Arabia intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone south of the Islamic holy city of Mecca on Tuesday evening, according to the spokesman of the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen.Turki al-Maliki said the targeting of Mecca, which is the home of Islam's most sacred shrine and the focal point of the Hajj pilgrimage, was a "disgraceful act".The 57-nation Organisation of Islamic Cooperation said attacks on Mecca and Medina province, where Islam's second holiest shrine is located, constituted an "unacceptable and intolerable transgression". But the Houthis, an Iran-backed armed group that controls much of western Yemen, denied targeting Mecca and accused Saudi Arabia of "fabrications and lies"."There is no threat whatsoever from Yemen to the holy sites. Our operations target their oil facilities and military bases, and are far removed from the holy places," military spokesman Yahya Sarea said.Sarea added that the Houthis had launched drones and missiles at Saudi Arabia in retaliation for more than 450 Saudi air strikes on their territory over the past week.He also said they had shot down a Saudi fighter jet over Marib province. There was no immediate response from the Saudi-led coalition, but Maj Gen Maliki did say that its forces would "not hesitate to take the necessary and deterrent measures against the terrorist Houthi militia and its hostile and terrorist behaviour". On Tuesday, Saudi authorities issued a series of brief security alerts for incoming projectiles in a number of western areas, including Mecca and Jeddah, the kingdom's second largest city.Meanwhile, the US embassy in Saudi Arabia issued a "reconsider travel" advisory, warning that Houthi attacks had targeted cities, infrastructure, airports, military bases, diplomatic facilities and energy facilities.The Houthis have recently seized control of large swathes of Yemen's Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed pro-government forces.Last week, they captured the strategic port city of Mokha and Perim Island in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the southern gateway to a key shipping route that links Asia and Europe via the Red Sea and the Suez canal.The Houthis said they posed no threat to international shipping but reiterated that they would target vessels from Saudi Arabia, which has relied on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.At the same time, Saudi Arabia's key East-West Pipeline, which was being used to transfer crude oil from the Gulf to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, had to be closed after it was badly damaged in a strike that the kingdom blamed on Iran-backed militias in Iraq. Some experts have said it could take more than a month to repair the pipeline, but US Energy Secretary Chris Wright predicted on Tuesday that oil should be flowing through it within days.Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the country's de facto ruler, has personally pressed US President Donald Trump to take military action against the Houthis, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News, the BBC's US media partner.Trump has so far declined to involve the US military directly, offering instead to assist with intelligence and targeting support, the sources said.A senior Trump administration official told the BBC: "We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen government regarding regional stability."The United Nations Security Council held an emergency meeting on Tuesday, during which both Yemen's government and Saudi Arabia called for more decisive action against the Houthis, who they accused of choking the Bab al-Mandab Strait as a way of applying economic pressure. Council members agreed that freedom of navigation in the Red Sea must be maintained to prevent disruption to global supply chains. More than 90,000 people have been displaced in Yemen by the fighting between the Houthis and pro-government forces, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM)."Families are being forced to flee for the second or third time in this conflict, with almost nothing left," Amy Pope, the IOM's director general, warned last week.The World Health Organization (WHO) said on Sunday that at least 500 people had been reported killed since the start of August, including 297 over the previous week.Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.The fighting has reportedly left more than 150,000 people dead and triggered one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, with more than 22 million people in need of some form of aid, according to the UN.A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

schema.headline: Saudi Arabia says it shot down Houthi drone south of Mecca

title: One dead after torrential rain and flash floods hit Barcelona region
description: North-eastern Spain has been hit by torrential rain and flash floods, leaving one person dead and causing widespread disruption across the region.Spai
body: North-eastern Spain has been hit by torrential rain and flash floods, leaving one person dead and causing widespread disruption across the region.Spain's national weather agency AEMET issued warnings for heavy rain across eastern regions on Wednesday, including a red alert for Barcelona's coastline.Rescuers recovered the body of a man on Thursday in Olivella, around 40km (25 miles) west of Barcelona, after his car was swept away by a stream, authorities said.The deluge has disrupted travel across Catalonia and Valencia, with flights cancelled and roads submerged. Authorities have advised against unnecessary travel, while Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez warned of "very complicated situations".Emergency services in Catalonia said they received more than 850 calls related to the downpours and catalogued over 500 incidents.Catalan firefighters said on X on Thursday that they had recovered the "lifeless body of a man" in Olivella, correcting earlier reports that had identified the missing person as a woman.Videos shared on social media showed partially submerged cars and rescue workers attempting to reach a vehicle trapped in a heavily flooded underpass.In Barcelona, some metro stations were closed and buses diverted, while regional trains were disrupted and flights delayed or cancelled at El Prat airport.Neighbouring Valencia had more than 70mm (2.76in) of rain fall in just half an hour in several municipalities, according to AVAMET."Rarely have we seen such rainfall accumulations in 30 minutes," the meteorological association said on X.Emergency services reported 478 incidents in the Valencia province, mostly involving property damage, leaks and traffic disruption. In the regional capital, all metro lines were suspended and the city's airport shuttered for several hours, causing flights to be diverted.

schema.headline: One dead after torrential rain and flash floods hit Barcelona region

title: Saudi Arabia: Satellite image reveals major damage that shut crucial oil pipeline
description: Satellite imagery shows a key oil pipeline in Saudi Arabia has been badly damaged after a strike last week, which experts have told BBC Verify could t
body: Satellite imagery shows a key oil pipeline in Saudi Arabia has been badly damaged after a strike last week, which experts have told BBC Verify could take more than a month to repair and force oil prices even higher.The image shows the most significant damage is at a pumping station along the East-West Pipeline, which Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on to export crude oil via the Red Sea rather than through the Strait of Hormuz, where ships have been attacked by Iran and the US during their six-month war.The Saudi government has accused Iranian-backed militias in Iraq of the pipeline strike, which followed days of renewed missile and drone attacks on south-western Saudi Arabia by Yemen's Houthi group - which is also backed by Iran. Saudi Arabia has retaliated by carrying out strikes on Houthi-controlled areas of western Yemen.New satellite images also show damage to Saudi Arabia's King Khalid Air Base after a Houthi strike last week.The Saudi government said on Tuesday it would respond "firmly" to attacks by the Houthis.While the Houthis have been fighting a long-running civil war against Saudi-backed Yemeni pro-government forces, the group has stepped up its campaign in recent weeks.It seized control of significant new territory across Yemen's south-western coast last week, including areas overlooking the crucial Bab al-Mandab waterway, strengthening its ability to enforce its declared blockade of Saudi shipping.

schema.headline: Saudi Arabia: Satellite image reveals major damage that shut crucial oil pipeline

title: What weapon could the US have put into space?
description: The announcement by the United States that it has deployed a space weapon in Earth's orbit has raised questions about what weaponry is actually in spa
body: The announcement by the United States that it has deployed a space weapon in Earth's orbit has raised questions about what weaponry is actually in space, and what role it could play in efforts by great powers to dominate that arena.Washington has given away little in its announcement. Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the "on orbit" weapon was necessary to safeguard US forces against hostile enemy action, but gave no details about the weapon's capabilities or when it was put into orbit.So what could this weapon be, and what is the wider picture like for military developments in space? Who else could have similar weaponry?Space has been a militarised domain since the start of the space age - in the late 1960s, the Soviet Union deployed weapons up there. The Istrebitel Sputnikov (IS; Satellite Destroyer) programme was made up of satellites that were designed to release projectiles that detonated, releasing shrapnel into the path of another (usually American) satellite.Nowadays, advanced militaries deploy satellites in space for a range of purposes, including reconnaissance, secure communications, detecting missile launches and providing precise location information for targeted strikes.As warfare becomes more technologically advanced, analysts expect the use of military hardware in space to increase.Dr Bleddyn Bowen, an associate fellow in military sciences at the Royal United Services Institute and associate professor in astropolitics at Durham University, said he was only able to hazard a guess about the weapon announced by the US."I would expect there to be some kind of electronic warfare or radio-jamming platform, possibly, this would be a non-destructive kind of anti-satellite weapon," he told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.Such weaponry already exists on Earth and can disrupt satellite communications, he said. "If you take out the radio links then your satellite is very useless."Bowen also would not rule out a riskier and more disruptive type of weaponry, which could create debris and destruction."Less likely would be a kinetic kill vehicle of some sort, so a vehicle that would release a projectile that could ram into a satellite and destroy it," he said.A type of "close inspection and grappling satellite would be another possibility as well."But while the weapon placed in orbit may be unusual, the US - and indeed its Russian and Chinese rivals - have had weapons that can be pointed and shot into space for some time.In a later BBC interview, Bowen was dismissive of China's reaction to the US announcement which warned against an arms race in space, describing it as "the pot calling the kettle black"."If you're already an expert... you know how hollow those words are coming from the Russian and Chinese governments," he said."The United States, Russia and China and also India have all developed different kinds of anti-satellite or counter-space weapons, and Russia and China have put a lot of technologies in space which have a lot of weapons potential," he added.In fact in the past 10 years, Russia and China have been doing a lot more manoeuvres in space, known as rendezvous and proximity operations (RPOs) - "buzzing" Western satellites."Theoretically, these RPO [satellites]can become hunter-killer satellites by physically colliding with them or by nudging them out of orbit," Dr Rod Thornton, reader in Russian Defence and Security Studies at King's College, London, told the BBC.Bowen added that the Chinese have demonstrated "space tug capability", saying: "A vehicle can go up to a satellite, can grapple it and move it into a different orbit."This, he said, could be a positive development - a way of removing space junk as well as knocking out working satellites.However, some types of space weaponry also have the potential to create huge amounts of space junk.Dr Mark Hilborne, a specialist in space security and weaponisation at King's College,  said direct ascent anti-satellite missile tests, such as one carried out by China in 2007, leave a great deal of debris in orbit for a very long time.Suess said debris from that test was still in orbit and still dangerous."It doesn't have to be a sort of huge piece of metal to do any damage, it can be a tiny piece of plastic, given the velocity that we're talking about in orbit," she said.Thornton said that what Russia lacks in space weaponry and satellites, it makes up for in missile capability."The Russians... have ground-based missiles which can be launched into space to strike [satellites] in low Earth orbit. They also have ASAT [air-launched antisatellite] missiles that can be launched from a great height by aircraft," he said."From the Russian point of view, they see Nato as having much better and more satellites than the Russian military can call up, therefore they have invested heavily in ASATs in order to 'level the battlefield' somewhat."Thornton added a sobering thought: "As a last resort, the Russians can also launch nuclear weapons into space and the EMP [nuclear electromagnetic pulse] blast would 'fry' any unhardened satellite over a wide expanse."So what is the likelihood of a nuclear conflict in space? Only if it was happening on the ground as well."What could happen in space is not something that would happen in isolation, really," Bowen said. "Nothing could happen, or something could."Given that weapons for use in space have been around for so long, why did the US announcement come when it did? Experts agree that it's not a major development as such, more a political signal.Bowen suggested that it could be a response to Chinese developments."China has modernised its military forces over the past 30 years," he said. "It has put a lot more military satellites in space and has presented a lot more targets that are worth the American military going after and hitting.""There's much more incentive for American space weapons now because China has a lot of vulnerability to space in the same way that the Americans have."This situation seems to have created a curious imbalance.Thornton said that, Russia would be the "big winner" in any space war, because it has so few satellites, unlike China and the US. It would involve "missiles fired up into space, manoeuvring satellites designed to nudge/destroy them and ground-based lasers," he said.

schema.headline: What weapon could the US have put into space?

title: US interest rates raised for first time in three years
description: US interest rates have been raised for the first time in more than three years and could be increased further in a bid to slow rising prices.Rates wer
body: US interest rates have been raised for the first time in more than three years and could be increased further in a bid to slow rising prices.Rates were hiked to 3.75%-4% from 3.5%-3.75% by the Federal Reserve in a unanimous decision, despite fierce opposition from President Donald Trump, who had called for rates to be cut.Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said the move was because "inflation is too high and has been for too long", adding that it was a "sober" and "responsible decision".After the announcement, Trump expressed support for Warsh but said the Fed board, which votes on rate decisions, was "hostile".Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive for people wanting to secure loans, mortgages, and credit cards, but can lead to better returns on savings.Warsh said during a press conference on Wednesday following the decision that, while there was "an attitude of optimism" within the Fed leadership, inflation remained a problem.Like many central banks, the Fed has a target of keeping inflation at 2% or below. Warsh noted that US inflation has been above the target "for more than five years".That has helped make affordability one of the top concerns of American voters, who have seen fuel prices surge in response to soaring wholesale oil prices since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran. This has driven up the cost of many goods and services, as well.While the Fed "cannot affect any individual price – whether it be oil prices, whether it be food stuffs at the grocery store", Warsh said, the central bank can work to keep  price rises from broadening across the economy.He added that strength in the jobs market and wider economy meant the Fed was staying focused on stabilising prices, and that those least well off had the most to gain from lower inflation.Central banks tend to increase rates when inflation is high to discourage spending and encourage saving, in the hope this will reduce the pace of price rises. But it's a balancing act, as higher rates can also encourage businesses to hold off on investing and hurt economic growth.When he was confirmed, Democratic lawmakers had said Warsh would be Trump's "sock puppet" and many Fed watchers expected him to carry out Trump's persistent demands to slash rates. Trump had been heavily critical of Warsh's predecessor Jerome Powell for not cutting them.Asked on Wednesday about the message the rate hike sent to Trump, Warsh chuckled before saying: "I have got nothing for you on a discussion with the president."Trump told reporters later "I'm relying on Kevin [Warsh], but he's got, you know, a very tough board"."And the, interest rates are too high. They're not appropriate... I talked to Kevin and I said, 'you might as well vote with the board because it's not going to matter.' The board is very hostile, they're very political," he added.Earlier, Trump said on social media: "LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!"Democrats on Capitol Hill said the rate increase would make loans costlier and, in turn, more Americans would go into debt."This is going to make everything become more expensive," said Chuck Schumer, the top Democrat in the Senate. "This is because Donald Trump does not know how to manage the economy."The Fed's hike is the first rate move in any direction since they were cut in December 2025. The last time they were raised was in July 2023. The increase could help push up mortgage rates for home buyers and lead to Americans paying more on other types of debt.Major US banks JP Morgan, KeyCorp, and BNY all raised their prime lending rate on Wednesday to 7% from 6.75%, which will affect rates charged on credit cards and personal loans.Mortgage costs have climbed over the past year but remain below peaks seen in 2023. A 30-year fixed deal is 6.76% on average, while a 15-year deal is 6.09%, according to figures from Freddie Mac.Many US homeowners have 30-year and 15-year fixed-rate mortgages, and changes to interest rates will not impact their monthly repayments. But higher rates could affect those looking to secure a new mortgage or refinance.Warsh declined to provide his own view on where he saw the Fed's rates going, but the majority of his fellow policymakers said they believe rates would be hiked again before the end of this year to between 4-4.25%. A small majority also said rates could rise further to the 4.25-4.5% next year, before cuts begin in 2028 and 2029. The forecast suggested price rises will ease in the coming years, with inflation, the measure used to assess the cost of living, predicted to fall steadily to the Fed's target by 2029.The US Fed is not alone in facing rising inflation since the Iran war, with the European Central Bank raising rates last week and the Bank of England set to make its own decision on Thursday.

schema.headline: US interest rates raised for first time in three years

title: Snapchat open to putting time limits on teens, boss tells BBC
description: The boss of Snapchat-parent Snap Inc says the firm would be "willing to implement" time limits for teens, following a call from Meta for it to take ac
body: The boss of Snapchat-parent Snap Inc says the firm would be "willing to implement" time limits for teens, following a call from Meta for it to take action.Evan Spiegel told the BBC in an interview at the company's California headquarters that setting a maximum amount of time that young users could spend on the app could be "an important step forward for the industry." His comments came as Snap revealed a slew of new features for its upcoming Specs glasses, which it said could connect to Apple iPhone and Mac devices.Meta has been pressuring other social media companies to join it in making platform changes it agreed to as part of a recent multi-billion dollar legal settlement with US states.Instagram and Facebook-parent Meta was facing allegations from Attorneys General for most US states who said the firm deliberately designed its apps to be addictive to young users.It agreed to pay $12.7bn and implement a two-hour daily limit for teen users across its platforms by default, in addition to muted notifications during school hours, blocks at night and other measures."I think it is an important step forward in the industry in terms of really identifying industry norms, and I think that would be beneficial overall," Spiegel told the BBC. "We've looked really thoughtfully at the terms."As part of Meta's August settlement, the company said it would implement even more stringent time limits and pay an additional $5.3bn if YouTube and TikTok follow suit. It has denied any wrongdoing as part of the deal, which will be paid over a 10-year period.Last month, a Meta spokesperson said it was hopeful that Snap would make similar platform changes as well.Meta, YouTube, TikTok and Snap have all faced a barrage of litigation alleging their apps have helped spawn a youth mental health crisis. Snap has also been accused of facilitating illegal drug sales.When asked about the idea of a default time limit, Spiegel said: "I think that's a really good example of something that that we'd be willing to implement."But Spiegel did not commit to a timeline on when Snap might take action. "That's something we've talked about internally," he said. "I don't have more to share today."He noted that Snap offers tools through its Family Center feature, which currently enables parents to track aspects of how their teens are using Snapchat."We want to figure out how we can be part of the solution," Spiegel added.YouTube-parent Google said it had no comment when asked if it planned to implement the measures in Meta's settlement. TikTok did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.Spiegel was talking to the BBC as Snapchat's parent Snap Inc announced new features for its upcoming Specs glasses.He said the smart eyewear would use AI to suggest things for people to do based on what the tech learns about their goals, relationships and routines. "Rather than the way that people use chatbots today where you constantly have to ask for stuff, Specs can understand what's important to you, and then offer recommendations or offer next steps," he said.Like other smart glasses, Specs will use AI to let people see digital elements overlaid onto the world.But the tech won't come cheap - retailing at $2,195 in the US and £1,995 in the UK."The target audience right now is early adopters of tech and developers as well as enterprise," Spiegel said.With the device, Snap aims to offer a middle ground between VR headsets like Meta's Quest 3 and lightweight AI smart glasses offered by rivals which look more like conventional glasses."We're creating a totally new category here," said Spiegel. "You have a really powerful computer that brings a lot of the immersive capability you see with VR, but they're also lightweight at just about 130 grams, so they're very wearable and they have these see-through lenses, so you can use them out in the world."Specs is Snap's most recent foray into the wearable tech, coming a decade after its short-lived Spectacles cost the company tens of millions of dollars.The device is also arriving as Meta is facing a significant backlash over its own smart glasses, which are estimated to be the most popular of the market.Some online derisively call them "pervert glasses" over how they have been used to secretly film women, with one person telling the BBC they were filmed leaving the beach, while another said they were told to pay to remove a video of them from the internet.Nevertheless, sales continue to rise. With seven million pairs having been sold according to Meta.Snap said it has built into the design of Specs, which do not use facial recognition to identify people.A white light flashes at the top of the glasses above the users nose when it is recording video and taking a photo.The company says that will let people nearby see that recording is happening.Users of Meta glasses have figured out ways to obscure components meant to indicate that a photo or video is being captured, including by tampering with the electronics in the device.Meta says it has remotely disabled the cameras on thousands of its devices on which tampering or destruction of the indicator light was detected.

schema.headline: Snapchat open to putting time limits on teens, boss tells BBC

title: Why Trump is all-in on AI despite the warnings
description: Figure caption, Why is Donald Trump so opposed to regulating AI?ByNorth America correspondentAccording to Donald Trump, concerns about the dangers of
body: Figure caption, Why is Donald Trump so opposed to regulating AI?ByNorth America correspondentAccording to Donald Trump, concerns about the dangers of artificial intelligence technology – that "robots will be marching into our cities and getting rid of us all" – are a hoax.It's the kind of language the US president typically reserves for the objects of his most intense derision – theories about human-driven climate change, investigations into Russian election-meddling, and the drives to impeach and remove him from office during his first presidential term.Styling himself as the "hoax buster", in a series of social media posts on Monday he issued a full-throated endorsement of what he called "the greatest economic development engine in history" and scorned those who doubted the benefits of the technology.The ranks of doubters have been growing in recent weeks, however, amidst anxiety over the disruptive nature of AI - if not worries about potentially civilisation-threatening danger - among some industry insiders and politicians, including from within Trump's own Republican Party.None of that has deterred Trump, however, whose latest social media fusillade was only his latest effort to turn back growing AI scepticism through sheer force of will. Whether the president views the AI fight as pivotal to his economic legacy, a key battleground in a global struggle for power, or another example of his enemies conspiring against him, he has, by fully joining the fight, elevated the issue to the forefront of American politics. That is even at the risk of crossing longtime allies."We think this could be a great technology, but we're not going to give these guys a carte blanche," former Trump adviser Steve Bannon said at a "pro-human" conference on the dangers of AI on Tuesday. "There's been no debate."Just before Bannon spoke, democratic socialist Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont told the same crowd that Washington policymakers had not addressed the "potentially catastrophic consequence" of unregulated AI."Congress under both Democratic and Republican control has been asleep at the wheel," he said. "And now we have a president whose ignorance regarding this issue is truly embarrassing."Figure caption, Watch: "Great" or "alarming" - Should AI be reined in?According to Trump, however, what's needed isn't debate or new policies, it's trust in his authority and judgement."The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades," he wrote. "We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies."A desire for centralised presidential authority is a familiar theme for Trump in his second term in office. If he decides something is good, he should have the authority to allow it; if he deems it bad, he ought to be able to end it by unilateral presidential order.It's similar to his outlook on immigration and trade. He believes that he, as president, should have the sole power to decide who can enter and remain in the country, and when and where to impose tariffs.Unlike tariffs and immigration, which have been issues of interest for Trump for decades, the rise in artificial intelligence technology is a recent development.But if this is no long-time, deep-seated interest on the part of the president, what could explain his willingness to press ahead?The 'hottest' economy and the driving force of AITrump regularly likes to tout America as the "hottest" country in the world. Many economists indicate that investment in AI technology – including infrastructure and equipment – has been the driving force in the US economy for several years. According to a recent report by the forecasting firm ING, tech investment accounted for more than a third of all US economic expansion in the second quarter of 2026.The stock market is booming, and much of that rise in corporate value (and, by extension, surging retirement portfolios of many Americans) can be attributed to the massive spending on computer chips, data centres and the other infrastructure behind AI.Anything that threatens this growth, which Trump considers to be a hallmark of his presidency and a key to his political legacy, quickly draws his suspicion.Trump also sees the AI expansion as a large-scale industrial competition between the world's two largest economies, the US and China. In the zero-sum game of global power, if China is ahead, then America is behind."We're leading China in AI," Trump said on Saturday, "and frankly, I want to keep it that way, because whoever wins AI wins."The president often touts a familiar conservative view that his opponents on the left are against the free market and economic liberties, and rely on alarmism to justify greater government intervention and control.Of course, Trump – who touts partial US ownership of US Steel and the semiconductor manufacturer Intel, and has no qualms about picking winners and losers in the American economy – is hardly a traditional small-government conservative.Tech bosses vary in views - and their access to TrumpTrump's close ties to prominent tech moguls and AI entrepreneurs from the start of his second term may also help explain his AI evangelism. Tech entrepreneur David Sacks, a co-chair of the president's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology and his informal AI tsar, has been a longtime supporter. Sacks's publicly aired scepticism of AI regulation mirrors recent comments made by the president."I think this is becoming a panic," he said this weekend in an interview with CBS News. "We're in an election season, and there is an incentive for political actors to try and amplify the fear."Elon Musk, despite a rocky relationship, has shaped the direction of this administration. Mark Zuckerberg of Facebook, Amazon's Jeff Bezos, OpenAI's Sam Altman and former Apple head Tim Cook all had prominent seats at Trump's inauguration.These men, along with Anthropic head Dario Amodei, hold a range of views on the necessity of greater AI regulation, and have differing levels of access to, and influence on, Trump.In Amodei's case, his conflicts over the Pentagon's unrestricted use of Anthropic's AI models could have negatively affected Trump's evaluation of Amodei's calls for a slowdown in AI development."This is the most prominent debate in the entire industry and has been since the beginning," said Matt Calkins, head of the tech firm Appian. "We knew it would spill into politics at some point because it had to."Figure caption, Watch: AI needs a 'brake pedal', Anthropic co-founder tells BBCWhere the political debate goes from here is an open question.With Trump's resistance, it is unlikely that Congress – despite promises of new hearings and proposed regulatory controls – will enact new legislation that Trump would sign into law. On Tuesday, Republican Speaker of the House Mike Johnson appeared to back away from earlier openness to congressional action, instead echoing Trump "AI hoax" rhetoric.With midterm congressional elections looming, candidates running for office – both Republicans and Democrats – are wary of ending up on the wrong side of public opinion that, according to polls, is sceptical of the promised benefits of AI advances.But Republicans are also wary of crossing Trump on an issue that has become a political touchstone for the president.Even though the public is starting to pay attention, Calkins says that the issue has not yet become political dynamite, which means political rhetoric comes with little risk. The moment when AI warnings turn into a high-profile disaster, however, could be looming."It is possible that events in the future might electrify the public, and then positions - and talk - might not be so cheap," he said.Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's weekly US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

schema.headline: Why Trump is all-in on AI despite the warnings

title: OpenAI's Sam Altman says world 'right to be afraid' but 'should trust' AI firms
description: The boss of ChatGPT-maker OpenAI says people should have more faith in AI firms to keep the tech safe, amid rising public concerns about the risks."Th
body: The boss of ChatGPT-maker OpenAI says people should have more faith in AI firms to keep the tech safe, amid rising public concerns about the risks."The world should trust that we are going to do the right thing because it's the right thing and we feel the magnitude of this," Sam Altman said on Tuesday during a conference in San Francisco.He accepted people were justified in being concerned about AI, as the capability of the tools has progressed rapidly.But critics say firms cannot be trusted to self-regulate, with left-wing Senator Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon, a former adviser of US President Donald Trump, among those calling for greater governance of AI.Trump himself has criticised calls for more guardrails on the fast-moving technology, calling fears about AI's safety a "hoax".He said the only "guardrails" needed for AI was a "strong and smart" president.Altman's comments on Tuesday came during an appearance at an annual conference hosted by software firm Salesforce. "It doesn't take as much imagination as it used to for [us] to imagine how this could go wrong," he said. "I think the world is right to be afraid of this."   But AI bosses themselves have also admitted it may be difficult to regulate a technology which is changing so quickly.In an interview with Axios published on 3 September, external, Altman said he had expected Congress to create a "basic framework" for advanced AI after his 2023 testimony, but that has yet to happen.He suggested lawmakers have struggled to keep pace with the technology and to regulate it without "slow[ing] down innovation".New safety legislation on AI is unlikely to emerge from the US Congress anytime soon, despite the fact lawmakers returned from their summer break on Monday.There is a lack of consensus within both US parties on how any regulation would happen - and the House is set to enter recess again at the end of the week ahead of the midterm elections in early November.Altman's comments on Tuesday were the first time he had spoken publicly since a post went viral last week by a researcher who quit the AI firm Anthropic. The researcher claimed AI could "kill all humans" by the end of the decade if left unchecked.A handful of other AI executives and experts responded by saying they agreed with the assessment, though they didn't explain how they came to their conclusions or how exactly AI could accomplish such a thing.After Altman's comments, Mark Zuckerberg wrote on X, external that every AI firm had the ability and the incentive "to take its own actions" towards safety."Any lab that doesn't focus on alignment will fall behind," the Meta chief executive wrote. "Labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this as well."Alignment is a field which aims to build human ethical ideas and principles into AI. In other words, it aims to keep it on track with what humans value.Some political figures have pushed back against the view that AI firms should be able to self-regulate.Bernie Sanders said decisions about AI had been left to "a handful of the richest people in the world", while former White House strategist Steve Bannon said the public could not trust tech oligarchs to regulate themselves.Nvidia boss Jensen Huang said at the same conference on Tuesday that AI firms should decide if new versions of the technology should be released - and not be managed by outside forces."We don't need new laws or regulations," he said, adding there should not be a "false choice" between the speed of innovation and the safety of AI products.Nvidia is the biggest company in the world by valuation, with its profits having boomed as a result of rampant demand for its hardware.Huang also argued  safety is an "engineering problem" and  companies should "take a pause" if they lose confidence in a product.The recent claims from inside the industry have intensified scrutiny of AI development, prompting Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei to call for the pace of AI development to slow, external and urge governments to regulate the industry.The post was applauded by Altman, Google's DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis and Elon Musk.By Tuesday, however, more AI leaders were voicing support for self-regulation rather than government involvement.Altman said AI companies were capable of regulating themselves."We will get it right," Altman said, adding that if firms could not keep "alignment and safety way ahead of capabilities" they would "slow down or stop".But Yoshua Bengio, one of the pioneers of modern AI, posted on X, external "ambitious efforts outside the for-profit sector" were needed to "avert the worst risks from AI".

schema.headline: OpenAI's Sam Altman says world 'right to be afraid' but 'should trust' AI firms

title: Russia's elections will have few surprises, but for the Kremlin they matter
description: Figure caption, Low expectations that Russia's election will bring peace closer, Steve Rosenberg reportsBySteve RosenbergRussia editorReporting fromMo
body: Figure caption, Low expectations that Russia's election will bring peace closer, Steve Rosenberg reportsBySteve RosenbergRussia editorReporting fromMoscow and DmitrovThe system of power in Russia is often referred to as "managed democracy" (where the Kremlin does the managing).That means huge powers for the president and few political surprises.This weekend's election is set to deliver another parliament dominated by the party of power, United Russia, and a house of MPs fiercely loyal to Vladimir Putin.Critics dismiss the vote as neither free nor fair.But the Kremlin doesn't care what the critics say."We have our own political system, our own political process," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov explained recently.That means no curveballs for the Kremlin. No surprises. So no story?Far from it.For the Kremlin, the election of 450 deputies to the lower house of parliament, the Duma, is important. This is the first parliamentary election here since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The Kremlin will use it to claim that most Russians back the president and the war, as well as to promote the political careers of soldiers back from Ukraine: officials say nearly two hundred war veterans are taking part in the election.Image caption, This election is being used to promote the political careers of some military veteransAs for the election campaign, that has provided a window on Russian society four-and-a-half years into the war.I said no surprises. But there have been some."Good evening and welcome to tonight's campaign speeches by candidates for Duma Electoral District 158," said the anchor on state TV.The studio director cut to a wide shot revealing six empty lecterns."The candidates haven't turned up," admitted the host. "So, it's goodbye from me."In another TV debate (where the politicians were present) one crooning candidate sang his pitch:"The Communist Party, onwards we go!"We're with the people, don't you know?"More X Factor than exit poll.Yet a musical manifesto is strangely appropriate. In the previous Duma, everyone seemed to be singing from the same hymn sheet. At the final session of parliament in July, MPs stood and applauded as the speaker of the house chanted repeatedly:"Russia, Putin, Victory! Russia, Putin, Victory!"It was a signal that all MPs in parliament should back President Putin and the war.Image caption, Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov [centre] backs the war in Ukraine"All parties in the Duma, every single one, voted in favour of 170 laws to support the special military operation," Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov told me with obvious pride about the last parliament."In that sense there is 100% agreement in the Duma."I caught up with Zyuganov on the campaign trail outside Moscow at a bread and biscuit factory. As I watched rows of identical-looking loaves speeding along the conveyer I thought about Russia's parliament. It's not that all parties in the Duma are identical: some are more nationalist, others – like Zyuganov's party - more left-wing. But when it comes to backing the Kremlin's legislative initiatives and supporting the "special military operation" they vote the same way. Such "systemic" parties are vital cogs in Russia's Kremlin-centric political machine.And if a party doesn't support the war?One such party - Yabloko - is calling for a ceasefire in Ukraine. Back in July it was the only anti-war party in Russia to be registered for the election. Twelve days later, though, the Supreme Court removed it from the ballot. That was widely interpreted as a sign of Kremlin concern that anti-war messaging could strike a chord with Russian voters.Despite Yabloko's exclusion from the party list, some of its candidates are still running in individual constituency races. Though in recent weeks growing numbers of Yabloko candidates have been detained by police, prosecuted for various offences and barred from the election."The police are carrying out a political order. That's no secret," Yabloko candidate Grigory Grishin tells me. "This way, the authorities are setting the boundaries within which they believe the elections should take place."It is well known that the demand for an end to the bloodshed in this conflict with Ukraine is very popular. In my opinion, most people in Russia now want peace and Yabloko helped people express this. That's why it's been excluded from the party lists, and why individual candidates are being barred."Image caption, Grigory Grishin says he believes demand for an end to the bloodshed in the conflict with Ukraine is very popularFor now, Grigory remains a candidate. But the police recently came to his flat."Three policemen in civilian clothes asked me to accompany them to the station, which I did. The police said I had posted what they claimed was an extremist symbol: the word 'Navalny' and that, by doing so, I had propagandised extremism via my Telegram channel."Alexei Navalny was Russia's most prominent opposition leader and Kremlin critic who died in prison in 2024. He'd been convicted on several charges, including extremism.The Russian authorities insist that the Duma elections are transparent and fair. Critics of the vote point to opposition politicians who have been forced into exile or put in prison. Last year one of the leaders of a prominent independent election monitoring group in Russia was jailed for five years. Grigory Melkonyants was convicted on charges of working with an "undesirable organisation". His election monitoring group, Golos, has shut down.Fifty miles from Moscow, in the town of Dmitrov, I see little sign of an election.In the town centre there's a memorial to "Heroes of the special military operation": local people killed fighting in Ukraine.The war is front and centre of people's minds here.Image caption, Olga's son-in-law is fighting in Russia's "special military operation""We feel it," says Olga, whose son-in-law is a soldier in the "special operation". "Because of the people who've gone to fight and the families left behind with sons, husbands, children and grandchildren there. But these elections can't influence what will happen.""I'd like us to live in a peaceful country, with no war," Polina tells me, "So that you don't have to worry that a drone will fall down in front of you."Russians have other concerns, too. Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil refineries have sparked widespread fuel shortages, while economic pressures are increasing."What worries me," says a barber called Ivan, "is that no matter how much you earn it's not enough. Prices are rising faster than wages. I speak to lots of people in my job. I know how hard-up they are."Expectations are low that this election will change much."Western elections and elections in Russia are completely different things," Grishin explains. "Elections in the West are a way of forming a government, which is replaced later if voters aren't satisfied."Elections in Russia never bring a change in government. At best, they're a way of influencing it, of sending a signal. But power in Russia never changed because of an election. That's how Russia is."

schema.headline: Russia's elections will have few surprises, but for the Kremlin they matter
